idiom_name: list[Callable[[Event], None]] with subscribe/unsubscribe and a notify copy
implementation_notes: Python has no Observer in the standard library, so the idiom is a plain list of callables on the subject: subscribe appends, unsubscribe removes, notify iterates over a copy so a handler may unsubscribe safely. The Observer interface disappears because a subscriber is any callable, and weakref.ref/weakref.WeakMethod - documented precisely for mappings that must not keep their referents alive - are how the registry avoids owning its observers. Reach for the class hierarchy only when observers must expose more than the update operation.
pitfalls: A bound method stored directly in the list keeps its instance alive (the subject now owns the observer); store weakref.WeakMethod and drop dead references during notify instead.
Iterating the live list while a handler subscribes or unsubscribes raises RuntimeError ('list changed size during iteration') or skips handlers - iterate over a copy.
One handler raising aborts the remaining handlers unless each call is isolated in try/except; decide the policy explicitly and log the failures.
The GIL does not make compound state updates atomic: a subject touched by several threads still needs a lock, and calling handlers while holding it can deadlock.

variants.name: framework signal dispatcher (Django/blinker style)
variants.idiom_name: named Signal objects with connect(receiver, sender=...) and send()
variants.implementation_notes: Framework dispatchers replace the per-object registry with module-level named signals: receivers connect to a signal (optionally filtered by sender) and the sender calls send(), so publisher and subscriber never import each other. Django's implementation stores receivers as weak references by default (weak=False opts out) and needs dispatch_uid to avoid duplicate registration, and its documentation warns that signals only *appear* loosely coupled and are harder to debug than direct calls. Use it for cross-application extension points, not for a subject with one obvious listener.
variants.code_sketch:
from django.dispatch import Signal, receiver
price_changed = Signal()                      # module-level, no subject import

@receiver(price_changed, sender=PriceTicker, dispatch_uid="warn_low")
def warn(sender, price, **kwargs): ...

price_changed.send(sender=PriceTicker, price=77.0)   # notifies all receivers
pitfalls: Receivers are weak references by default: a local function or transient object is garbage-collected and silently stops receiving - pass weak=False when the receiver must stay alive (the Django docs call this out).
Import-time registration plus reloads register the same receiver repeatedly, so a signal is handled twice; guard with dispatch_uid (or connect once in an app-ready hook).
Global signals are invisible in the call graph: add sender filtering, otherwise every receiver in the process reacts to every send - including other tests' senders.
dispatch is synchronous and in-process: a slow receiver blocks send(), and exceptions propagate into the sending code.
